title: Poems in the dark
hook: in prison he composes his great love poem in his head

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Toledo cell: a closet, a slit of light, nine months. Your line was the dark room. Who did you hold in mind that can't leave theirs? Today, what John did in there. Day two hundred fifty-eight.

If someone locked you in a closet for months, no phone, no books, no paper, what would your mind do? Most of us would replay every wrong ever done to us. We'd plan revenge, or despair, or both. John of the Cross, cold and sick in his cell in Toledo, did something else. He started making poems. Not angry poems. Love poems. He had nothing to write with, so he composed them in his head, line by line, and kept them there, memorized, in the dark. Some of the most beautiful poetry ever written in Spanish began that way. Today's word is that work.
screen: `NO PHONE, NO BOOKS, NO PAPER.` → `NOT REVENGE. LOVE POEMS.` → `MEMORIZED IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: First, the Canticle. The biggest poem he began there is known as the Spiritual Canticle. It's a love song, modeled on the Song of Songs in the Bible. A bride searches everywhere for her beloved, who has slipped away. For John, the bride is the soul and the beloved is God. He made about thirty stanzas in that cell, keeping them in memory. Second, the kind jailer. After some months, a new, younger friar was put in charge of him. He was gentler, let John out to empty his bucket, and at some point gave him a pen and a little paper. That's how some of the poems survived. Third, the spring. One of the poems from the cell has a refrain that keeps coming back, in John's Spanish: "Que bien sé yo la fonte que mana y corre, aunque es de noche." How well I know the spring that rushes and flows, although it is night. Think about where he wrote it. No light. No news. And he says: I know where the water is. Even now. Even at night. Fourth, the psalms. He wasn't making it all up from nothing. Like every friar, he had the psalms by heart from years of praying them. When everything else was taken away, what was inside his memory was still his. The Bible's love poetry and the psalms' cries were the raw material. In the Douay-Rheims: "For though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, for thou art with me." What you've memorized can't be confiscated.
screen: `A LOVE SONG FOR THE SOUL.` · `A KIND JAILER, A LITTLE PAPER.` · `I KNOW THE SPRING, THOUGH IT IS NIGHT.` · `WHAT YOU KNOW BY HEART STAYS.` · then, large: `AUNQUE ES DE NOCHE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: memorize one line of a psalm. Try this one: though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, for thou art with me. Say it once slowly. Then again, with your eyes closed. Then once more, only in your head. If you pray, let it be a prayer. If you don't, let it be something to carry that no one can take. By the bell, it's yours. The bell holds the time.
Poems in the dark. In his Toledo cell, John composed love poems to God in his head, among them the Spiritual Canticle and the song of the spring at night. Today's word.
Your line: songs in prison. Today, say your psalm line from memory at least three times: waking, midday, and before sleep. Day two hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Carmelites and many other Catholics read and pray John's poems, especially the Spiritual Canticle, and memorizing psalms and short scripture verses remains a common Catholic devotional habit.

fork.setup: you're locked in a dark closet for months with nothing to read or write with. what do you do with your mind?
options: replay every wrong done to you.
compose love poems in your head and memorize them.
sleep as much as you can.
fork.reveal: John made poems, some of the most beautiful ever written in Spanish, and kept them in memory until he had paper.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saint who wrote some poems.
what it means: a prisoner in the dark, making love songs to God in his head, because memory was the one thing left to him.
what a scholar hears: about thirty stanzas of the Spiritual Canticle, the poem of the fonte, and the romances on the Trinity are usually dated to the Toledo imprisonment.
